newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea catalytic converter prices seen up on PGMs.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea catalytic converter prices seen up on PGMs.

text.p: South Korean catalytic converter makers said on Tuesday they see surging world platinum group metals (PGMs) prices feeding through into the domestic market in the fourth quarter, but do not expect supply disruptions.
Average converter contract prices are forecast to rise by about 20 percent to 30,000 won per unit between October and December from the 25,000 won agreed in the third quarter.

Prices for platinum and palladium, used in the manufacture of catalytic converters, have soared to seven-year and 17-year highs respectively on world markets recently due the disruption of Russian contract shipments.
But South Korean metal dealers said they have seen no signs that local converter producers, with long-term PGM supply contracts, are concerned about their shipments.
"We have never seen these companies buying the white metals in the domestic market," one dealer with a bullion house said.
The quarterly contract pricing system based retrospectively on PGM prices for the previous three months means catalytic converter prices have barely changed so far this year.
"We have not seen any change of supply and demand in the domestic market," said a senior official with Heesung Engelhard Corp, one of South Korea's two major converter makers.
The company is a joint venture between Engelhard Corp and South Korea's Heesung Group, which was spun off from the LG Group in 1995.
The second company, Oriental Degussa Co Ltd, is a joint venture between German Degussa AG and South Korea's Oriental Chemical Industries Co Ltd.

Since 1993, when South Korea ruled all vehicles should be fitted with catalytic converters and use lead-free gasoline, auto makers have had no choice but to purchase the devices, which filter harmful gases and particles from car exhaust.
"Demand for catalytic converters is expected to fall slightly this year due to a slowdown in the domestic economy, especially the labour unrest in January," an official at Oriental Degussa said.
Local car makers including Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, Kia Motors Corp and Daewoo Motor Co Ltd, were also seen shrugging off skyrocketing PGM prices.
"We have not seen any impact on our auto production from the PGM price increases," a spokesman for Daewoo Automotive Components Ltd said.

The source at Oriental Degussa said the use of palladium in catalytic converters, newly introduced in the domestic market from last year, has rapidly been replacing platinum due to the attrative price differential.
Platinum was fixed at US$410 an ounce in London on Tuesday morning morning, while palladium fixed at $210 an ounce.
The two white metals are generally used in a ratio of 5:1 to rhodium in catalytic converters. Rhodium, another PGM, was quoted at between $330-$370 an ounce in London on Tuesday.
Platinum/rhodium catalytic converters are expected to account for about 70 percent of South Korea's total output this year and and palladium/rhodium the remaining 30 percent, Oriental Degussa said.
The spokesman said the figures were forecast to be reversed in 1998 with platinum's share falling to 30 percent.

This compared with 90 percent platinum/rhodium and 10 percent palladium/rhodium last year, when South Korea's total catalytic converter production was estimated at 3.5 million units, the spokesman added.
Imported catalytic converters make up only about five percent of the country's total market, he said.
According to data by the Korea Automobile Manufacturers Association (KAMA), South Korea's car production totalled 2,812,714 vehicles in 1996 and was expected to reach 3.0 million vehicles in 1997.
In 2000, South Korea's car production was projected to reach 3.5 million vehicles, an official with the KAMA said.
-- Seoul Newsroom (822) 727 5651
